analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from secretly surveilling workers' union activity, off-duty life, and health, and requires disclosure of all monitoring.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee on June 18, 2026, and no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar employers with 11 or more workers from collecting or using worker data to track union organizing, whistleblowing, off-duty activity, political or religious views, or health conditions unrelated to the job, and from monitoring workers in restrooms, break rooms, lactation or prayer rooms, or their own homes. It would require employers to tell workers exactly what data is collected, how, and how it feeds hiring, firing, discipline, and performance decisions. Workers would get the right to see and correct their data, employers could not sell worker data or hand it to third parties, and a new Labor Department division would enforce the rules, backed by worker lawsuits with damages up to $40,000 per violation and a ban on forced arbitration of those claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at covered employers (11 or more workers) and job applicants, plus labor unions, whose organizing activity would be protected from data-driven detection.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and job applicants at covered employers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits using worker data to identify or monitor people who have or intend to join or assist a labor organization, or to engage in protected concerted activity.
Bars collection of worker data while off-duty in break rooms, restrooms, locker rooms, lactation or prayer rooms, or the worker's own home or remote work location.
Bans employers from selling or licensing worker data and from transferring it to third parties, and requires opt-in consent plus cybersecurity protections before transfer to a service provider.

Requires employers to disclose what data is collected, how, how often, who has access, and how it affects decisions on hiring, firing, discipline, scheduling, wages, and promotion — and gives workers a right to review, correct, and request reconsideration of data-driven work decisions.
Prohibits retaliation against workers who exercise these rights or complain, and makes predispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers unenforceable for claims under the bill.

Creates a Worker Protection and Technology Division in the Department of Labor with advisory boards including labor representatives, and a private right of action with statutory damages of $5,000–$20,000 per violation of the data rules ($10,000–$40,000 for willful or repeated violations).

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 11 or more workers and the vendors that sell employee-monitoring and workforce-analytics tools, which face collection limits, disclosure duties, data-sale bans, and lawsuit exposure.

drawbacks.text: The definition of employee data is sweeping — covering routine HR files, productivity metrics, communications, device usage, and online activity — and the 11-employee threshold captures many small employers, so compliance and recordkeeping costs would be substantial even for firms with modest surveillance programs.

The bill's permissible-use standard requires data collection to be 'strictly necessary' and the 'least invasive means' available, which could force employers to abandon productivity, quality, and safety monitoring tools that many businesses and some workers view as legitimate.

Statutory damages per worker, a private right of action, and attorney-fee awards create substantial litigation exposure, and the honest cost of strong data rules is that some disputes will be settled by lawsuits rather than fixes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The worker protections are real and targeted: union-spying, restroom and home monitoring, and sale of worker data are practices most people would not accept if disclosed. The bill is carefully structured — it preserves stronger state laws, keeps routine performance assessment legal, and deletes data on a timeline. The main honest objections are cost and breadth: the data definitions are broad enough to sweep in ordinary HR practices at small firms, and the damages-plus-fees structure will produce litigation. On balance, the protections for workers outweigh the compliance burden, though a narrower data definition and a higher employee threshold would reduce the cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee on June 18, 2026, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote — the typical path for a bill introduced with no opposition-party support in the closing months of a Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced the Stop Spying Bosses Act on June 18, 2026, joined by seven original cosponsors — six Senate Democrats and one Independent, Sen. Bernie Sanders.

The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; the full action history shows no further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action.
The 119th Congress runs until January 3, 2027, so the bill remains technically alive, but no vote has occurred and none is scheduled.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers that monitor workers and the vendors selling workforce-surveillance tools are better off, because the bill has not advanced and the practices it targets remain unregulated at the federal level.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and surveillance vendors, so far

sides.party_line_note: All eight initial supporters are Senate Democrats or the independent who caucuses with Democrats; none of the 55 Senate Republicans has cosponsored, and no vote has yet been held.

industries.note: These firms sell productivity tracking, keystroke and location monitoring, and algorithmic management tools, and some buy or resell worker data. The bill bans selling worker data, requires opt-in consent for transfers, restricts what can be collected, and mandates disclosure — directly shrinking a growing market.

Employers with 11 or more workers face collection limits, plain-language disclosure duties, workers' rights to see and correct their data, and lawsuit exposure with damages up to $40,000 per violation. Their interest in continuous productivity and behavior tracking runs against workers' privacy in this bill.

The bill makes it illegal to use data collection to identify or monitor union organizing or protected concerted activity, and gives unions standing to sue over violations. Unions also hold seats on the new division's advisory boards.
The bill voids predispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for claims under the Act, moving worker-surveillance disputes from private arbitration into open court.

analysis.trajectory: Introduced with no Republican support roughly six months before the Congress ends, with no committee action and no scheduled hearing or markup, the bill is very unlikely to advance further in the 119th Congress; the realistic path is reintroduction in the next Congress.
